newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Witchcraft militia group spearheads war in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Witchcraft militia group spearheads war in Zaire.

text.p: In the war in Zaire the frontline force is a highly volatile tribal witchcraft group -- the Mai-Mai -- who believe bullets turn into water if their chief has innoculated the target with a secret vaccine.

The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), fighting to topple ailing strongman Mobutu Sese Seko, is using the Mai-Mai as psychological shock troops to frighten off ill-disciplined Zairean soldiers.

The rebels now control much of eastern Zaire after capturing the towns of Uvira, Kamanyola, Bukavu, Goma, Butembo and Beni. The rebels and the Mai-Mai are now knocking on the doors of Bunia and Kisangani -- Zaire's fourth largest city.
The Mai-Mai army has children as young as 10 years old and their main motive for fighting seems to be loot.
The ADFL rebels have trucked thousands of Mai-Mai warriors to the frontline near the town of Bunia and are relying once again on their supernatural powers to overwhelm army troops.
The Mai-Mai take their name from the Swahili word for water and fight in family groups armed with weapons including rifles, crossbows, slingshots, spears and home-made shotguns.

At a roadblock outside Beni, a seven-year-old Mai-Mai child in a red beret and oversized camouflage trousers tries to draw his personal weapon, a chrome-plated plastic cutlass, from its sheath, but it is nearly taller than him.
At another roadblock, another child slithers down a mud bank under the weight of a 12 kg (26 lb) Belgian FN assault rifle, hundreds of rounds of ammunition wrapped around it.
Behind him, a 10-year-old wearing only khaki shorts and a grass headband carries a carbon-fibre crossbow as he begs for cigarettes and food.
Hundreds of such sights are common through much of the northern front of rebel-held eastern Zaire.

On Sunday Mai-Mai child warriors captured the village of Mambasa, which lies astride the Bunia-Kisangani highway, effectively cutting off Bunia and some 5,000 Zairean soldiers there from any escape route.

Bunia is the rebels' next target on the northern front as they extend the territory they have carved out of eastern Zaire over the past seven weeks. Last week they said they had captured the town but this turned out to be premature.
A group of Mai-Mai children at a roadblock in the war zone near Beni looked astounded on Monday when asked if they would rather go to school or fight the Zaireans.

"Why be at school when you have to defend your village?" said 12-year-old Tafunde Watale, wearing purple sprigs in the epaulettes of his camouflage uniform, grass round his forehead and a hot and cold mixer tap around his neck.

"We defended our village against the Mobutu fighters, now we are going to finish them further away. The Banyamulenge (rebels) have told us we can loot what we want in Bunia, and then stay behind," he added.
An ADFL rebel commander who declined to be named admitted there were disciplinary problems with the Mai-Mai and would not comment on the need to use child fighters.
The conflict in eastern Zaire began when the government tried to expel the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group which migrated to Zaire from Rwanda up to 200 years ago.
The Banyamulenge, backed by Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army, resisted the expulsions by taking up arms and formed an alliance with other Zairean opposition groups including the Mai-Mai.
